name: Normalcy bias
statement: People meeting a warning of disaster read it inside their ordinary expectations, underrate the danger, and act late or not at all.
meaning: The claim is about interpretation rather than fear. A siren, a tremor or a smell of smoke arrives as an ambiguous signal, and the reading that fits an ordinary Tuesday beats the reading that would require leaving the building. Yamori, summarising Hirose's 1984 formulation, describes two forms. The first pushes an abnormal event into a familiar frame so that its strangeness is discounted. The second appears when the announced danger is far past what anyone could cope with, and the ambiguity in the announcement is used to rate the risk low. Both are claims about one moment, the moment a person is told something bad is coming. Testing them needs a measure of what that person believed at that moment. Most of what is offered instead is a record of what they did afterwards.

origin.where: The Japanese Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
origin.note: The phrase appears in the English abstract of a laboratory experiment on how fast a subject, left alone after working under different styles of leadership, responded to an unexpected alarm bell. That is the earliest journal article located, not a coinage. Two fire-safety documents read for this entry, Kuligowski's NIST Technical Note 1619 and Kinateder, Kuligowski, Reneke and Peacock's 2015 review, both credit the term to Keizo Okabe and Shunji Mikami, in a paper on the socio-psychological effect of a false warning of the Tokai earthquake given at the Tenth World Congress of Sociology in Mexico City in August 1982. That paper was not obtained and is known here only through those two citations of it. Yamori's 2009 review traces the Japanese concept, 正常化の偏見, to Hiroyoshi Hirose's 1984 book 生存のための災害学, which was not obtained either. Who first put the English phrase in print could not be established.

evidence: The sociology of warning response does not use the term, and the fire-safety engineering literature does. Mileti and Sorensen's 1990 review for Oak Ridge National Laboratory synthesised more than 200 studies, and the Department of Energy catalogue record for it gives 235 references. Its third major conclusion, stated in those words, is that confirmation of warnings underlies the entire warning response process: most people answer a first warning by seeking more information, calling friends and relatives, and waiting to hear the message again. The report lists that fifth among the myths in a section headed Myths That Confuse Goals, whose first item is that the public panics. Drabek had described the same sequence in 1969 from interviews with 278 families evacuated before a Denver flood in June 1965, separating warning, confirmation and evacuation as distinct processes. Averill and colleagues found it again at the World Trade Center. Their NIST investigation ran 803 telephone interviews with survivors, 427 from WTC 1 and 376 from WTC 2. In WTC 1 the most common reported delay before leaving the floor was one minute or less in all three zones; the median was three minutes below floor 43 and on floors 43 to 76, and five minutes on floors 77 to 91. Seventy percent of WTC 1 survivors and 75 percent of those in WTC 2 talked to others before leaving. The causal model gave an adjusted explained variance in evacuation delay of 49 percent in WTC 1 and 56 percent in WTC 2. Its largest path in both towers was taking pre-evacuation actions, at .47 and .51. The three strongest direct effects after that were environmental cues, floor, and information received without being sought. Seeking further information had a small direct effect on delay, .10 in WTC 1 and .11 in WTC 2, and worked instead through the actions people took to get ready. Kuligowski and Mileti published the path analysis separately in 2009. The phrase normalcy bias occurs in none of those documents. It does occur in the fire-safety literature, where Kuligowski's 2008 NIST technical note and the 2015 review define it as the predisposition to read a cue as though nothing is wrong.

replication.headline: Nothing repeats the bias under its own name, and the evacuation experiments that test the same mechanism agree that a calm bystander stops people leaving and disagree about whether it slows down those who do.
replication.detail: Under the name there is nothing. Searches on 17 August 2026 at Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the SHARE index of OSF preprints return case reports, commentary and one modelling paper, and no experiment that takes the bias as its object. PubMed holds five records containing the phrase, the earliest Omer and Alon in 1994. Under another name there is a literature. The mechanism the term describes, reading an ambiguous emergency cue as ordinary because the people nearby are treating it as ordinary, has been run as an experiment several times under the heading of social influence on evacuation. Kinateder and Warren tested 150 people one at a time, half in a real laboratory and half in a matched virtual room seen through a head-mounted display, with a fire alarm sounding ten minutes into a bogus matching task. Three further volunteers were dropped for technical or procedural errors, and the six groups held 25 each. Seventy-three walked to the exit: 38 in the active bystander condition, where a confederate looked at the alarm and left, 26 in the control condition, and 9 in the passive bystander condition, where the confederate glanced at the alarm and carried on working. In a logistic regression the passive coefficient was -2.75, 95% CI -4.39 to -1.39, p < 0.001, and the active coefficient 1.69, 95% CI 0.16 to 3.66, p < 0.05. The negative influence was weaker in the virtual room, interaction coefficient 2.17, 95% CI 0.30 to 4.19, p < 0.05, and 68 percent of the virtual group thought the alarm was part of the experiment against 20 percent of the real group. Where the results part company is on delay rather than on the decision. Among the 73 who left, bystander condition and environment had no effect on pre-movement time, chi-square(2) = 2.85, p = 0.24. Kinateder, Müller, Jost, Mühlberger and Pauli, on 40 people in a virtual smoke-filled tunnel with four conditions, report that pre-movement and movement times in their passive condition were delayed against all the others, and their abstract calls that difference statistically reliable. Yamori's 2009 review argues a third way, that the bias is not strong when people actually face an alert and is built afterwards. Latané and Darley's 1968 smoke-filled room is the ancestor of the paradigm, and its figures of 75, 38 and 10 percent reporting the smoke are quoted here from Kinateder and Warren's introduction, because the 1968 article was not obtained.

study.cite: Kinateder, M., & Warren, W. H. (2016). Social influence on evacuation behavior in real and virtual environments. Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 3, 43.

limits: The searches behind that verdict, run on 17 August 2026, were: Crossref by bibliographic query for the phrase and for evacuation delay, milling, warning response and passive bystander experiments; PubMed, which holds five records containing the phrase, the earliest from 1994; Europe PMC, which returns 58 records for the phrase and 28 when evacuation or experiment is added; the SHARE index over OSF preprints, which returns five items and no experiment; and Crossref lookups for every DOI cited here. Full-text searches were made of five technical documents. The phrase appears in three of them and not in Mileti and Sorensen 1990, the NIST report on World Trade Center occupant behaviour, or Quarantelli's 2001 encyclopedia article on panic. Several things could not be read. J-Stage returned a 500 error all afternoon for the 1988 article, so its abstract and its sample size could not be re-read on this pass, and the 1988 date rests on the Crossref record and on the earlier reading. Okabe and Mikami's 1982 conference paper and Hirose's 1984 book are known here only through citations of them. Drabek's 1986 inventory, the first item in Wikipedia's reference list, is a book and was not obtained. Latané and Darley's 1968 article was not obtained. Nilsson and Johansson's 2009 cinema evacuation experiments in Fire Safety Journal were located at Crossref, and neither the article nor an abstract from a primary source could be reached, so nothing from them is used here. Ripley's 2008 book was not read, only her 2005 article, and time.com refused every direct request, so that article was seen through one rendering rather than two. OpenAlex was out of quota and no count from it is quoted. A previous version of this entry said the 2015 fire-evacuation review was paywalled. It is open access at Fire Science Reviews under a Creative Commons licence, and it was read in full for this pass.
misreadings: The split usually quoted as 10-80-10 has a traceable source and no data under it. Leach's 2004 paper in Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine gives 10 to 15 percent who remain relatively calm, about 75 percent who are stunned and bewildered, and 10 to 15 percent who show counterproductive behaviour. Leach introduces the three groups as consistent with previously reported natural histories of disasters, citing his own 1994 book, and the third group carries four references: Edwards 1976, Glass 1959, that book, and Singer 1982. His method was a reading of witness testimony, survivor debriefings and inquiry reports from shipwreck and aircraft emergencies. Ripley named him in Time in 2005 and gave the first group as 10 to 15 percent and the third as 15 percent or less, which is not quite his wording. The figure attached to normalcy bias specifically, that 80 percent of people show it, is Wikipedia's, taken from a 2013 Gizmodo article that gives 70 percent and cites no study for it. Freezing and panic are separate claims carrying separate evidence. Quarantelli's review reports that most scholars agree the phenomena are statistically quite rare, usually involve only a handful of persons, and are of short duration, and that some researchers find clear-cut cases hard to find in disasters, so the claim that panic is uncommon is the one the sociology supports. That most people freeze is a different claim and rests on the testimony analyses above. Milling is not paralysis either. It is the information seeking documented since Drabek's flood families, and NIST found seven of every ten survivors of WTC 1 talking to others first. The six-minute average quoted for the World Trade Center is a mean on a right-skewed distribution: NIST gives a modal delay of one minute or less and a tail of people who took more than half an hour. The ostrich effect at entry 118 is a different effect, about how often investors check accounts they expect to show losses, and the bystander effect at entry 146 rests on the 1968 seizure study rather than the smoke-filled room used here.

sources.text: Yamori, K., & Misumi, J. (1988). The effects of leadership behavior in the normal time on follower's coping behavior when emergency occurred: An experimental study. The Japanese Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 28(1), 35-46. Earliest print use of the phrase located in this search; it appears in the English abstract and keywords.

Yamori, K. (2009). Revisiting the concept of normalcy bias. The Japanese Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 48(2), 137-149. Argues the bias is weak at the moment of the alert and is constructed after the event; credits Hirose (1984) with the formulation.

Mileti, D. S., & Sorensen, J. H. (1990). Communication of emergency public warnings: A social science perspective and state-of-the-art assessment. ORNL-6609. Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Full text read from the OSTI copy; source of the third major conclusion on confirmation and of the section headed Myths That Confuse Goals. The phrase normalcy bias does not occur in it. The count of 235 references is from the OSTI catalogue record, not from the report.

Averill, J. D., Mileti, D. S., Peacock, R. D., Kuligowski, E. D., Groner, N., Proulx, G., Reneke, P. A., & Nelson, H. E. (2005). Occupant behavior, egress, and emergency communications. NIST NCSTAR 1-7. Full text read; source of the 803 interviews, the delay quartiles in Tables 6-7 and 6-15, the milling percentages, and the path coefficients and adjusted explained variance in Appendix C. The phrase normalcy bias does not occur in it.

Kuligowski, E. D., & Mileti, D. S. (2009). Modeling pre-evacuation delay by occupants in World Trade Center Towers 1 and 2 on September 11, 2001. Fire Safety Journal, 44(4), 487-496. The peer-reviewed path analysis of the NIST interview data.

Kinateder, M., & Warren, W. H. (2016). Social influence on evacuation behavior in real and virtual environments. Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 3, 43. Open access; full text read. Source of the 150 participants, the 73 who evacuated, the condition counts of 38, 26 and 9, and the logistic regression coefficients.

Kinateder, M., Müller, M., Jost, M., Mühlberger, A., & Pauli, P. (2014). Social influence in a virtual tunnel fire: influence of conflicting information on evacuation behavior. Applied Ergonomics, 45(6), 1649-1659. Forty participants in a virtual smoke-filled tunnel; abstract read at Europe PMC, article not obtained.

Kinateder, M. T., Kuligowski, E. D., Reneke, P. A., & Peacock, R. D. (2015). Risk perception in fire evacuation behavior revisited: definitions, related concepts, and empirical evidence. Fire Science Reviews, 4, 1. Open access. Defines normalcy bias as reading cues as indicative of everyday events and credits Okabe and Mikami (1982).

Kuligowski, E. D. (2008). Modeling human behavior during building fires. NIST Technical Note 1619. Full text read; names normalcy bias as the predisposition to interpret the situation as if nothing is wrong, and gives the full Okabe and Mikami 1982 citation.

Latané, B., & Darley, J. M. (1968). Group inhibition of bystander intervention in emergencies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 10(3), 215-221. The smoke-filled room study. Not obtained; its figures are quoted in this entry only as Kinateder and Warren's introduction reports them.

Drabek, T. E. (1969). Social processes in disaster: Family evacuation. Social Problems, 16(3), 336-349. Interviews with 278 families evacuated before a Denver flood in June 1965; separates warning, confirmation and evacuation. Read as abstract and catalogue record, not in full.

Quarantelli, E. L. (2001). The sociology of panic. Disaster Research Center Preliminary Paper #283, University of Delaware. Written for the International Encyclopedia of the Social and Behavioral Sciences. Full text read; the phrase normalcy bias does not occur in it. The older /bitstreams/.../download form of this link now returns the repository's application shell rather than the PDF, and the address here is the one that serves the document.

Leach, J. (2004). Why people 'freeze' in an emergency: Temporal and cognitive constraints on survival responses. Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine, 75(6), 539-542. PMID 15198281. The proximate source of the 10-15 / 75 / 10-15 split. The PubMed record carries the abstract; the passage giving the three groups was read in two separately hosted reprints of the article.
Ripley, A. (2005). How to get out alive. Time, 25 April 2005. Attributes the term to disaster researchers, quotes Michael Lindell, and cites Leach's 2004 paper by name for the three-group split.

Omer, H., & Alon, N. (1994). The continuity principle: A unified approach to disaster and trauma. American Journal of Community Psychology, 22(2), 273-287. The earliest PubMed record containing the phrase; a theoretical paper, and its abstract carries no percentage.

Inglis-Arkell, E. (2013). The frozen calm of normalcy bias. Gizmodo, 2 May 2013. Source of the 70 percent figure that Wikipedia reproduces as 80 percent; it names four bodies of work and attributes the number to none of them.

National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2018). Emergency alert and warning systems: Current knowledge and future research directions, chapter 1. National Academies Press. Sets out milling and confirmation as the documented response; does not use the term normalcy bias.
Wikipedia, Normalcy bias. Used to find sources, not as one; its claims are described in this entry rather than relied on.
